extracted.intended_audience: students, scientists, and philosophers concerned with scientific method and inductive reasoning
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for judging the validity, applicability, and epistemic weight of inductive generalizations, probabilistic inferences, and comparisons of phenomena in scientific reasoning. Emphasizes limits of averages, combining evidences, transformation of approximations into universal statements, and the special status of mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply approximate generalizations only within observed limits
rubrics_metrics.description: If the proposition, 'Most A are B,' has been established by sufficient induction, we may conclude that any particular A is B with a probability proportioned to the preponderance of affirmative instances over exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This holds only within the limits of time, place, and circumstance embraced in the observations; numerical precision in the data permits corresponding precision in estimating error chances. A general average should only be applied to cases which are neither known nor can be presumed to be other than average cases (e.g., life tables useful for insurance but of limited use for judging any particular life). Such averages are the first term in a series of approximations; subsequent terms require appreciation of circumstances of the particular case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not apply genus averages to known species or specially-circumstanced individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: If we know that an individual instance i belongs to a particular species or variety of A, we shall generally err in applying to i the average struck for the whole genus; averages for the whole genus will mislead for any subclass or external circumstances not included in the average.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always prefer the average or generalization appropriate to the narrower class or to the set of external circumstances known to affect the particular instance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use numerical precision in data to measure chances of error
rubrics_metrics.description: If it has been practicable to attain numerical precision in the data, a corresponding degree of precision may be given to the evaluation of the chances of error in the conclusion (e.g., if nine out of every ten A are B, there is one chance in ten of error for an unknown A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify error probabilities only within the empirical scope of the observations; do not extend numerical probabilities beyond the observed domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish Addition vs Deduction when combining approximate generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: When two approximate generalizations are joined, they may (1) each be separately applicable (joining by Addition) giving a higher probability than either alone, or (2) one be applicable only via the other (joining by Ratiocination/Deduction) giving a lower probability than either.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize which mode applies in an argument (e.g., two independent witnesses = addition; hearsay-of-hearsay = deduction). Addition increases probability (if independent); deduction compounds uncertainty and typically reduces probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume independence for multiplicative combination; check for dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: The computation that multiplies complementary chances (e.g., 1/3 × 1/4 = 1/12 chance of not-B) presumes that the probabilities arising from A and C are independent of each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If A and C are connected (membership of one increases chance of membership of the other), independence fails and the joint probability cannot be computed multiplicatively; dependence can make joint evidence add no new support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chained approximate generalizations diminish probability multiplicatively
rubrics_metrics.description: When approximate propositions are chained (Most A are B; Most B are C; Most C are D...), the probability of the far-end conclusion diminishes at each step, approximately by multiplying the proportions (e.g., 9/10 × 8/9 × 7/8 = 7/10).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because experience underlying approximate generalizations rarely admits accurate numerical estimation, we often cannot precisely measure the diminution, but must remember that credibility dwindles with each illation; 'a hearsay of a hearsay' is worthless after a few removes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convert approximate generalizations into universal propositions with explicit provisos when exceptions are identifiable
rubrics_metrics.description: If the reason for stopping at an approximation is only inconvenience (not impossibility) and we know the character distinguishing exceptions, we may substitute a universal proposition with a proviso (e.g., 'All persons who have uncontrolled power employ it ill, provided they are not persons of unusual strength of judgment and rectitude of purpose').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record each proviso and carry it through the reasoning so that the aggregate of conditions appearing at the end exactly indicates the limitations and accumulated errors of the conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat approximate generalizations as effectively universal for mass-level inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: In inquiries about the properties of multitudes (e.g., politics, human society), it is generally enough to know that most persons act in a particular way, since speculations and practical arrangements refer to masses where what most persons do determines outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For policy or statistical planning affecting large groups, approximate laws may be used with the same assurance as universal laws for individuals, provided the target is a mass or an indefinite succession of individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove existence claims by linking to laws of succession or co-existence; a single positive instance suffices for general existence
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence of an individual phenomenon not directly perceived is inferred from inductive laws of succession or co-existence; general propositions asserting mere existence are often sufficiently proved by a single instance (e.g., a single authenticated sighting would establish that ghosts/unicorns/sea-serpents exist).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existence, for logic, refers to phenomena or possible states of consciousness; when within present observation, direct perception establishes existence; beyond that, inference must be from established inductive connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge resemblance by direct comparison or via a third object and applicable general propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: When direct juxtaposition is impossible or imprecise, compare each object with a third object capable of being transported between them, and reason by general propositions (e.g., 'Things which are equal to the same thing are equal to one another').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resemblance judgments should aim for detailed, part-by-part comparison where feasible; where not, use reliable intermediary measures or theorems (mathematical axioms where applicable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat mathematical laws of resemblance separately from empirical causal laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The only laws of resemblance independent of causation belong to mathematics (axioms of equality, inequality, proportionality); other empirical equalities or proportionalities are either derived from or identical with causal laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims of resemblance, distinguish whether the claim is mathematical (applies universally without regard to origin) or empirical (must be traced to causal laws and tested by induction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge mathematical axioms as inductive but empirically secure
rubrics_metrics.description: Elementary mathematical truths (e.g., 'Things which are equal to the same thing are equal to one another') are results of observation and experience—inductive truths—because they have been perpetually perceived true and never found false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these axioms as exceptionally reliable premises in deductive reasoning, since their continual confirmation makes them effectively universal for further deductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose uniform, simple definitions or modes of formation to facilitate arithmetic deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: It is advantageous to select a mode of formation for numbers which is alike for all (e.g., the place-value system conveys a simple uniform principle) because a known mode of formation for each number allows deduction of all other modes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defining basic concepts (like numbers), prefer definitions that fix a single, uniform connotation to enable straightforward deductive reasoning from minimal inductive premises.
